blocks.text: LLM 量化是指用比训练时更少的位数来存储大语言模型中的数值。如今大多数 LLM 使用 FP16 或 BF16，都是 16 位格式。fp8 把每个权重占用的内存减半，fp4 或 int4 则降到四分之一，这样同一块 GPU 就能装下更大的模型，或服务更多请求。代价是准确度，因为每个权重都会被舍入到更小格式能存储的最近值。

blocks.text: 量化主要有两类。训练后量化转换的是已训练完成的模型权重，可以是动态的，在运行时计算每个激活值的范围；也可以是静态的，提前用样本数据跑一遍模型算出这些范围。量化感知训练则在训练过程中模拟舍入，让权重学会适应这种误差。Hugging Face Optimum 概念指南对两者都有讲解，Transformers 量化概览则介绍了你可以自己运行的量化方法。

blocks.text: fp8 与 bf16：有什么区别？

inlines.text: fp8 与 bf16：有什么区别？

blocks.text: 浮点格式把位数分配给符号、指数和尾数三部分。指数决定数值范围，尾数决定该范围内数值的分辨精细程度。

inlines.text: 浮点格式把位数分配给符号、指数和尾数三部分。指数决定数值范围，尾数决定该范围内数值的分辨精细程度。

blocks.alt: Bit layouts: bf16 has 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 mantissa bits; fp16 has 1, 5 and 10; fp8 (E4M3) has 1, 4 and 3; fp4 (E2M1) has 1, 2 and 1.

blocks.text: bf16 有 1 个符号位、8 个指数位和 7 个尾数位，因此它的数值范围与 32 位 fp32 相同，但精度更低。fp16 把 16 位拆成 5 个指数位和 10 个尾数位。OCP 8 位浮点规范定义了两种 fp8 编码：E4M3（4 个指数位、3 个尾数位）和 E5M2（5 个指数位、2 个尾数位）。fp8 同时牺牲了范围和精度，所以量化模型会为每个张量或每组权重存一个缩放因子。MXFP4 每 32 个值共用一个缩放因子，NVFP4 则每 16 个值用一个 fp8 缩放因子。

inlines.text: 在我们的测试中，fp8 和 fp4 都没有测出质量损失。六个端点的得分都在 98.3% 到 99.2% 之间，而这样规模的测试无法排除一两个百分点的差距。

blocks.text: 我们把 280 个有精确答案的任务跑过 qwen/qwen3.8-27b，固定到六个端点。Cerebras 以 fp16 提供该模型，Parasail、CoreWeave 和 AkashML 以 fp8 提供，Darkbloom 和 ModelRun 以 fp4 提供。每个请求都设置 provider.only、quantizations 和 allow_fallbacks: false，因此只能到达我们指定的端点，温度为 0，关闭推理。任务包括带演算过程的多步算术、需要追踪的 Python 程序、对 20 到 30 个数字排序、在 240 或 1,200 个条目中查找一个键（约 4,000 和 20,000 个 token），以及一条穿过约 9,000 个 token 的四步查找链。所有任务都由我们生成，因此每个都有精确答案，不需要评审模型。另外 40 个任务要求直接给出两个四位数的乘积、不写演算过程，单独计分。

blocks.text: 没有任何任务类别能区分出不同精度。每个端点在任一类别中最多错两个任务，而且都是普通的失误，比如排序列表里漏掉一个数字。三个 fp8 端点彼此在 240 个任务中有 2 到 5 个不一致，两个 fp4 端点有 4 个不一致。Darkbloom 与 fp16、fp8 端点不一致的次数最多，有 7 或 8 个任务，但它的总分与 fp16 相差不到半个百分点。

blocks.text: 唯一出现差距的地方是不写演算过程的乘法。fp4 的 Darkbloom 在 40 个乘积中答对 26 个，而其他五个端点为 30 到 33 个，其中 fp4 的 ModelRun 是 30 个。针对最佳端点（33 个）做两比例 z 检验——这个比较是我们看到结果之后才选的——结果显示，在没有真实差异的情况下出现这么大差距的概率约为 7.5%，因此我们不能把它称为精度效应。各精度下答错的乘积都很接近，误差中位数不到 0.01%。

blocks.text: 并非所有权重都同等重要。AWQ 发现，保护约 1% 最重要的权重就能大幅降低量化误差；LLM.int8() 则采用混合精度，把离群值保持在 16-bit，而超过 99.9% 的数值以 8-bit 相乘。我们对 Qwen3.8 27B 的测试无法显示各家提供商用的是哪种方法，但 fp16 端点漏掉了 240 个任务中的 3 个，fp8 和 fp4 端点则漏掉了 2 到 4 个。

blocks.text: 当模型在 16-bit 下放不进你的硬件，或者你需要从同样的 GPU 获得更高吞吐量时，就该量化。在我们的测试中，没有发现 fp8 有精度损失，而且 fp8 对每个权重的舍入幅度比 4-bit 更小，所以它是更小的一步。请先在你自己的任务上测试其中任意一种。通过 API 使用时，你不需要自己量化模型，只需在 OpenRouter 上通过 provider.quantizations 选择一个提供你所需精度的端点。

blocks.text: When you call an open-weight model through an API, several providers may serve it at different precisions, such as 16-bit bf16, 8-bit fp8 or 4-bit fp4. The precision can affect both the answers and the price. LLM quantization creates these versions by storing a model’s weights in fewer bits, so the model needs less memory and hardware, at some cost in accuracy.

blocks.text: LLM quantization means storing a large language model’s numbers with fewer bits than it was trained with. Most LLMs today use FP16 or BF16, which are 16-bit formats. fp8 halves the memory each weight takes, and fp4 or int4 quarters it, so the same GPU holds a bigger model or serves more requests. The cost is accuracy, because each weight is rounded to the nearest value the smaller format can store.

blocks.text: There are two main types of quantization. Post-training quantization converts a finished model’s weights. It can be dynamic, computing the range of each activation at run time, or static, computing those ranges in advance by passing sample data through the model. Quantization-aware training simulates the rounding during training so the weights learn to tolerate it. The Hugging Face Optimum concept guide explains both, and the Transformers quantization overview covers the quantization methods you can run yourself.

blocks.text: fp8 vs bf16: what’s the difference?

inlines.text: fp8 vs bf16: what’s the difference?

blocks.text: Floating-point formats split their bits between a sign, an exponent and a mantissa. The exponent sets the range of values, and the mantissa sets how finely values within that range are resolved.

inlines.text: Floating-point formats split their bits between a sign, an exponent and a mantissa. The exponent sets the range of values, and the mantissa sets how finely values within that range are resolved.

blocks.alt: Bit layouts: bf16 has 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 mantissa bits; fp16 has 1, 5 and 10; fp8 (E4M3) has 1, 4 and 3; fp4 (E2M1) has 1, 2 and 1.

blocks.text: bf16 has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits, so it has the same range as 32-bit fp32 with less precision. fp16 splits its 16 bits as 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits. The OCP 8-bit floating point spec defines two fp8 encodings, E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits). fp8 gives up both range and precision, so quantized models store a scale factor per tensor or per block of weights. MXFP4 shares one scale across each block of 32 values, and NVFP4 uses one fp8 scale per 16 values.

blocks.text: We ran 280 tasks with exact answers through qwen/qwen3.8-27b, pinned to six endpoints. Cerebras serves it at fp16. Parasail, CoreWeave and AkashML serve it at fp8, and Darkbloom and ModelRun serve it at fp4. Each request set provider.only, quantizations and allow_fallbacks: false, so it could only reach the endpoint we named, at temperature 0 with reasoning off. The tasks were multi-step arithmetic with working, Python programs to trace, lists of 20 to 30 numbers to sort, a key to find among 240 or 1,200 entries (about 4,000 and 20,000 tokens), and a four-step lookup chain through about 9,000 tokens. We generated every task, so each has an exact answer and no judge is needed. Another 40 tasks asked for the product of two four-digit numbers with no working, scored separately.

blocks.text: The one place a gap showed was multiplication with no working. Darkbloom at fp4 got 26 of 40 products exactly right, against 30 to 33 on the other five endpoints, including 30 on ModelRun at fp4. A two-proportion z-test against the best endpoint (33), a comparison we chose after seeing the results, puts the chance of a gap that large arising with no real difference at about 7.5%, so we can’t call it a precision effect. To send a request to the cheapest endpoint that passes your precision filter, add :floor to the model slug, as our
explains. With quantizations: [“fp8”], qwen/qwen3.8-27b:floor went to Chutes, the cheapest fp8 endpoint, on both of our tries.

blocks.text: In our test, the cheapest full 280-task run was at fp4 and the most expensive at fp16, but the order in between didn’t follow precision. One run cost $0.58 on Darkbloom (fp4), $0.72 on AkashML (fp8), $0.77 on ModelRun (fp4), $0.81 on Parasail (fp8), $1.19 on CoreWeave (fp8) and $1.24 on Cerebras (fp16). Speed didn’t follow precision either. Cerebras (fp16) and ModelRun (fp4) answered in a median 1.3 and 2.4 seconds, against 8.4 to 15.0 seconds for the other four. Across all endpoints, median 24-hour uptime was 99.8% or higher at every labeled precision except fp32, which has one endpoint.

blocks.text: How do you choose the precision you get?

inlines.text: How do you choose the precision you get?

blocks.text: Check what a model’s endpoints serve, then set provider.quantizations on your requests. A GET to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/qwen/qwen3.8-27b/endpoints returns one entry per endpoint with its quantization, price, context length and uptime. It answered without an API key when we called it, and the model’s providers tab shows the same list. For Qwen3.8 27B it listed 21 endpoints, with one bf16, one fp16, ten fp8, three fp4 and six unknown. Check the count for the precision you want before you pin it, because that count is how many endpoints can take over when one fails.

import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"},
    json={
        "model": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of Australia? One word."}],
        "reasoning": {"enabled": False},
        "provider": {"quantizations": ["fp8", "bf16", "fp16"]},
    },
    timeout=120,
)
data = response.json()
if "error" in data:
    raise RuntimeError(data["error"])
print(data["provider"], data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"], f'${data["usage"]["cost"]:.6f}')
We ran it three times, and each run printed the same line.

blocks.text: quantizations filters the list of endpoints. We drop every endpoint whose precision isn’t in the list, then load-balance across the rest, weighted toward the lowest price, and fall back to the next endpoint if a provider fails. Nothing in the filter guarantees the same provider each time, so log the response’s provider field if you track quality. The docs also note that fp4 includes mxfp4 and nvfp4, and fp8 includes mxfp8.

inlines.text: Common problems with precision filters and how to fix them

blocks.text: The filter runs before any provider is contacted, so an empty candidate list fails fast. Asking Qwen3.8 27B for int8, which no endpoint serves, returned a 404 in 0.4 seconds.

The routing_funnel field shows how many endpoints survived each step, and failed_routing_step names the step that left none. {“quantizations”: [“fp8”], “only”: [“cerebras”]} returned the same 404 with quantization: fp8, because Cerebras serves fp16, so the funnel went from 21 endpoints to 1 to none.

blocks.text: Sort endpoints by quality signals with Exacto

inlines.text: Sort endpoints by quality signals with Exacto

blocks.text: Quantized quality depends “on the method used”, and each provider runs its own inference software, so two endpoints with the same label aren’t guaranteed to match. For requests with tools, Auto Exacto already moves endpoints with lower throughput, tool-calling success rates and benchmark scores to the back of the list. To apply that ordering to requests without tools, add :exacto to the model slug. Exacto ranks endpoints on tool-calling signals, not on accuracy at your task, so run your own prompts against the endpoints you’re considering. How to evaluate LLM provider performance covers how to compare their latency, throughput and uptime.

blocks.text: Is higher or lower quantization better?

inlines.text: Is higher or lower quantization better?

blocks.text: More bits keep more of the original model’s precision and take more memory. In our test of Qwen3.8 27B on October 20, 2026, we didn’t detect an accuracy difference between fp8, fp4 and fp16 endpoints on 240 tasks with exact answers. That covers one model on one day, so test 4-bit on your own workload before you commit to it.

blocks.text: Why doesn’t quantization destroy an LLM’s accuracy?

inlines.text: Why doesn’t quantization destroy an LLM’s accuracy?

blocks.text: Not all weights matter equally. AWQ found that protecting about 1% of the most important weights greatly reduces quantization error, and LLM.int8() uses mixed precision, keeping outlier values at 16-bit while multiplying more than 99.9% of values in 8-bit. Our test of Qwen3.8 27B can’t show which methods the providers use, but the fp16 endpoint missed 3 of 240 tasks and the fp8 and fp4 endpoints missed 2 to 4.

blocks.text: When should you quantize a model?

inlines.text: When should you quantize a model?

blocks.text: Quantize when the model doesn’t fit your hardware at 16-bit, or when you need more throughput from the same GPUs. In our test we didn’t detect a loss at fp8, and fp8 rounds each weight less than 4-bit does, so it’s the smaller step. Test either one on your own tasks first. Through an API you don’t quantize the model yourself. You choose an endpoint on OpenRouter that serves the precision you want, with provider.quantizations.

blocks.text: What does “unknown” quantization mean on a provider?

inlines.text: What does “unknown” quantization mean on a provider?

blocks.text: It means the provider hasn’t reported a precision for that endpoint. On OpenRouter, 865 of 1,455 endpoints were unknown on October 20, 2026, and 610 of those belong to closed-weight models such as Claude and Gemini. unknown is also an accepted value in provider.quantizations, so you can include or exclude those endpoints.
